newsitem.title: USA: U.S. medical team finds embargo hurts Cuban health.
newsitem.headline: U.S. medical team finds embargo hurts Cuban health.

text.p: The U.S. economic embargo on Cuba has had a devastating impact on the health of ordinary people on the Communist-ruled island, a team of U.S. medical experts said on Monday.
The U.S. State Department quickly challenged the report, saying that Cuba had other trading partners and the condition of its health system reflected its own national priorities.
"If there's a finger to be pointed about why the Cuban people don't have adequate medical supplies, it should be pointed directly at Fidel Castro," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Members of the American Association for World Health told a news conference that tightening the embargo in 1992 had stifled access to drugs and medical technology made by U.S. companies or their European subsidiaries.
The 1992 Cuban Democracy Act has licensing provisions for humanitarian exemptions, but in practice there are obstacles to getting food, drugs and medical technology to Cuba, they said.

"Our medical delegation found the tightening of the embargo has had unintended consequences on the health of the Cuban people, including unnecessary suffering and deaths," Dr. Peter Bourne, chairman of the association's board, said.
The private, nonprofit group did not blame all the problems of Cuba's healthcare system on the U.S. embargo.
They said there were "internal problems" in Cuba, including a severe economic crisis that would place strains on the health system even without an embargo.
But the State Department's Burns said that in 1995, Cuba itself reported that only $6 million of its $2 billion foreign exchange purchases were for medicine.
"It's a question of priorities. The Cubans have a ... command economy, they put resources into armaments for their military, and they choose not to spend money on their own people," he said.

The medical group, however, said that the embargo, imposed in the early 1960s to isolate Castro, made it virtually impossible for Cuba to get spare parts for medical equipment and denied it access to important drugs, ranging from the latest chemotherapy agents for cancer to ordinary painkillers for children.
"The cupboards were bare," said Dr. Robert White, a neurosurgeon at Case Western Reserve University, who was part of the delegation that went to Cuba.
Cuban hospitals "were rapidly becoming, indeed appearing like, medical museums," relying on equipment that was "10, 20 or even 30 years behind the times," White added.
The report found that in 1991, Cuban doctors had access to about 1,300 medicines but that has dropped to fewer than 900.
"We witnessed kidney dialysis, X-ray, respirators, incubators and other life-saving machinery standing idle for want of U.S.-produced spare parts," said Bourne.

Under U.S. law governing the embargo, licenses can be granted for shipments of food and drugs. But the process is so costly and cumbersome that some businesses are reluctant to even try to do medical business with Cubans, and others have faced complications and delays, the panellists said.
The water supply is also made with U.S.-made pipes and equipment, and water cleanliness has deteriorated, contributing to a rise in water-borne diseases, they said.
